name: Stanozolol

lead: Stanozolol (Winstrol) is an anabolic steroid that bodybuilders and athletes use for lean, dry, defined muscle. It became widely known through the 1988 Ben Johnson doping case.

It activates the androgen receptor, which helps retain muscle while water and softness drop, producing a hard, lean look. It is approved in the US for hereditary angioedema, where it raises liver production of C1 inhibitor, and is used in veterinary medicine. No controlled trial tests it for appearance in healthy people, and teen forum posts that ask about it for height are not backed by studies.

paras: It comes as an oral tablet and as an injectable, and users typically add it late in cutting phases alongside a calorie deficit and training. Users describe a drier, harder look developing over several weeks.

A study in weight lifters found oral stanozolol cut HDL cholesterol sharply; case reports and animal data describe liver injury, and reviews link anabolic steroids to cardiac deaths. It is US Schedule III and prohibited in sport. Anyone still growing should avoid it.

angle.text: Stanozolol (Winstrol) is a steroid used for a dry, lean, hard look: androgen signalling helps keep muscle while water and softness come off. It is approved for hereditary angioedema; forum posters also mention face and height, which studies do not address.

lead: Stanozolol, sold as Winstrol and in Europe as Stromba, is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid derived from dihydrotestosterone. In physique culture it is known as a cutting-phase compound used for a lean, hard, dry-looking muscular appearance, because it does not convert to estrogen and is described as causing little water retention.[1][2] It is orally active thanks to a 17-alpha alkyl group, and it has also been made as an injectable.[1]

Medically it was developed by Sterling-Winthrop in 1962 and has been used for hereditary angioedema, chronic venous insufficiency and, historically, osteoporosis, aplastic anaemia and growth disorders; veterinary versions are used in animals.[1] It is far better known for doping: it was among the first steroids banned by the IOC and IAAF (1974) and was the substance found in Ben Johnson's urine after the 1988 Olympic 100 metres final.[1][3]

Controlled research on appearance effects in healthy people is sparse. Published human studies focus on blood lipids in weight lifters, safety signals such as liver injury, and clinical uses in angioedema, venous disease and blood disorders.[4][5][6] In looksmaxxing forums it shows up mainly in threads by teenagers asking about height and about masculinising the face and body, a use no published study has tested.[7][8][9]
infobox: Hereditary angioedema prophylaxis; formerly osteoporosis, aplastic anaemia[1]
About 22% of DHT's; not a 5-alpha-reductase substrate; non-aromatizable[1]
About 9 hours oral; about 24 hours intramuscular[1]
US Schedule III (1990); Canada Schedule IV; banned in sport[1]

paras: Stanozolol is used to prevent attacks in hereditary angioedema, where it increases hepatic production of C1 inhibitor and complement component C4.[2] Wikipedia describes the long-term use as continuing to reduce attack frequency, though newer drugs for the condition have come to market since 2009; the hereditary angioedema literature likewise describes attenuated androgens as an older option now used less because of adverse events, with C1-inhibitor concentrates, icatibant and later drugs taking their place.[1][10]

It has also been used with some success for chronic venous insufficiency and the skin changes of lipodermatosclerosis, possibly speeding ulcer healing, and has been studied for osteoporosis, skeletal muscle injury and dermatological conditions.[1] A clinical study evaluated it after decitabine treatment in high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome and reported improved progression-free survival.[6] In veterinary practice it has been used to improve appetite and weight in dogs, cats and horses, with evidence described as weak.[2][1]

Bodybuilders use it to build lean mass without much water retention, often in cutting phases, and a 1989 survey examined AAS use among competitive bodybuilders.[2][11] Wikipedia notes that its lack of aromatisation and 5-alpha-reduction is linked to a higher anabolic-to-androgenic ratio than testosterone and no estrogenic effects.[1]

In looksmaxxing forums, posters ask about stacking Winstrol with other compounds to masculinise the face and physique or while 'heightmaxing'.[7][8][9] Those threads are discussed under the lore section; no published study has tested stanozolol for facial or height outcomes.

Stanozolol is an androgen receptor agonist with about 22 percent of the receptor affinity of dihydrotestosterone. It cannot be converted by 5-alpha-reductase and does not aromatise to estrogen.[1] A 1984 study compared its binding to androgen receptors in skeletal muscle and prostate and to sex hormone-binding globulin with other anabolic steroids.[12] In angioedema its effect is attributed to raising C1 inhibitor production in the liver.[2] Wikipedia also describes laboratory and animal findings involving the progesterone receptor, COX-2 and estrogen receptor alpha signalling.[1]

The oral half-life is about 9 hours and the intramuscular half-life about 24 hours, with a duration of action of a week or more for injectable preparations.[1] Urinary metabolites can be detected for up to roughly 10 days after a single small oral dose, which underlies its prominence in drug testing.[1] Chemically it is a 17-alpha-methylated androstane steroid with a pyrazole ring fused to the A ring; the 17-alpha alkyl group allows oral use and is associated with liver strain.[1][2]

Sterling-Winthrop developed stanozolol in 1962; it was sold in the US as Winstrol and in Europe as Stromba.[1] In 1970 the FDA's DESI review found probable efficacy only as an adjunct in osteoporosis and in pituitary dwarfism. The dwarfism indication was removed in 1980, and approval for osteoporosis and aplastic anaemia was withdrawn in 1984 after the FDA judged the data insufficient.[1]

Ownership then passed through several companies: Eastman Kodak bought Sterling in 1988, sold its drug business to Sanofi in 1994, and Sanofi's US manufacturer Searle stopped production in 2002. Ovation Pharmaceuticals acquired the drug in 2003, Lundbeck bought Ovation in 2009 and Lundbeck withdrew it from the US market in 2010; it can still be obtained through compounding pharmacies. Pfizer's veterinary authorisations moved to Zoetis in 2013 to 2014.[1]

The IOC and IAAF first banned stanozolol in 1974, and it has remained prohibited by WADA and USADA.[1] Anabolic steroids as a class have been the most frequently detected doping agents in IOC-accredited laboratories for many years.[13]

On 24 September 1988, Canadian sprinter Ben Johnson won the Olympic 100 metres final in Seoul in a world record 9.79 seconds. Park Jong-sei of the Olympic Doping Control Center found stanozolol in his urine sample, and Johnson was stripped of the gold medal and the record.[3] Johnson later admitted steroid use when he set his 9.83 record in Rome in 1987, which the IAAF also rescinded; he has at times suggested his drink may have been tampered with while also giving ambiguous statements about it.[3] His coach Charlie Francis wrote in Speed Trap that Johnson preferred furazabol and found stanozolol made his body feel tight, and testified at the 1989 Dubin Inquiry that Johnson had used steroids since 1981.[3][14]

The Dubin Inquiry, formally the Commission of Inquiry into the Use of Drugs and Banned Practices Intended to Increase Athletic Performance, was led by Charles Dubin, Chief Justice of the Ontario Court of Appeal. It heard 122 witnesses over 91 days beginning in January 1989 and reported in June 1990 with more than 70 recommendations, concluding that doping 'threatened the essential integrity of sport'.[15][3] Johnson admitted under oath that he had lied when he first denied doping.[3]

A 1989 JAMA crossover study gave 11 male weight lifters oral stanozolol or intramuscular testosterone enanthate for six weeks. Stanozolol reduced HDL cholesterol sharply, while testosterone had a different effect, supporting the view that oral administration is a key factor in the lipid change.[4] Earlier work examined reductions of lipoprotein(a) and of apolipoprotein D with stanozolol.[16] A 2010 study of weight lifters taking Decadurabolin and Winstrol for two months reported chromosome damage and cytotoxicity in oral mucosa cells.[17]

A 1977 controlled study examined long-term anabolic therapy in the elderly,[18] and a clinical study in high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome reported improved progression-free survival when stanozolol was added after decitabine.[6] No controlled trial of stanozolol for cosmetic muscle gain, facial change or height in healthy people was found.

Wikipedia lists virilisation, liver toxicity, cardiovascular disease and hypertension, and the drug has a diuretic effect.[1] Stanozolol is associated with liver injury: a case report described stanozolol-induced bland cholestasis and a randomised trial in cats reported hepatotoxicity.[5][19] Anabolic steroids as a class are linked to worsened cholesterol profiles, raised LDL and lowered HDL, peliosis hepatis, left ventricular hypertrophy, gynecomastia, testicular atrophy, virilisation in women and children, and psychiatric effects such as aggression and dependence.[13] The large HDL reduction seen in the weight-lifter study is a recognised cardiovascular concern, and a literature review covers sudden cardiac death in AAS users.[4][20]
Menstrual irregularities occur in women at maintenance doses.[2] Use by adolescents is flagged as a harm in reviews of the class.[20]

Stanozolol is a Schedule III controlled substance in the United States under the Anabolic Steroids Control Act of 1990, Schedule IV in Canada and Class C5 in Brazil; anabolic steroids are Class C in the UK and controlled in many other countries, which has created a black market of smuggled, counterfeit and clandestinely made products.[1][13] It is prohibited in sport and restricted in US horse racing.[1] Supplements have also been found cross-contaminated or faked with doping agents.[21]

Looksmax.org threads appear mostly from teenagers asking whether to keep running Winstrol and Superdrol while pursuing height, or whether Winstrol or Anadrol is better for masculinising the face and body.[7][8][9] One poster reports growing from about 157 to 165 cm in a year during use; a reply attributes the growth to puberty timing and says the compounds are more likely to limit height.[8] A T Nation thread notes that prescriptions at supraphysiological doses of such drugs sit in a legal grey area.[22]

lore.intro: Teen posters on looksmax.org ask whether Winstrol helps or harms height and whether to choose it or Anadrol to masculinise the face and body, while physique forums discuss it as a cutting compound.[7][8][9][22]

claims.claim: Winstrol and similar compounds help height growth.
Non-aromatising steroids are safe for growth plates.
Winstrol masculinises the face and physique.
Winstrol gives a dry, lean look without water retention.
Oral steroids like Winstrol are harder on the liver than injectables.
Elite athletes cannot compete at the top without steroids.

timeline.event: Developed by Sterling-Winthrop and marketed as Winstrol.[1]
FDA DESI review finds probable efficacy only for adjunctive osteoporosis and pituitary dwarfism.[1]
IOC and IAAF first ban stanozolol.[1]
FDA withdraws approval for osteoporosis and aplastic anaemia; binding-affinity comparison of anabolic steroids published.[1][12]
Ben Johnson stripped of Olympic 100 m gold after a positive stanozolol test (September).[3]
Dubin Inquiry begins; JAMA study reports sharp HDL reduction with oral stanozolol in weight lifters.[3][4]
Anabolic Steroids Control Act places stanozolol in US Schedule III; Dubin report released in June.[1][15]
Lundbeck withdraws it from the US market; compounding remains.[1]
Study reports improved progression-free survival with stanozolol after decitabine in high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome.[6]
